text: There are four rituals that I consider mandatory, and they operate at different time horizons. The first is daily exception triage. chapter: SEGMENT 2: Core Rituals and Cadence (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX

speaker: KEVIN
text: It's more nuanced than that. The output is a triaged queue with three categories. chapter: SEGMENT 2: Core Rituals and Cadence (10 minutes)

text: The weekly ritual is a model-and-workflow review. This is a sixty-minute session where you look at the performance of your AI systems at a higher level of abstraction than the daily triage. chapter: SEGMENT 2: Core Rituals and Cadence (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: And then you mentioned biweekly and monthly rhythms as well. Walk us through those.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: Core Rituals and Cadence (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: The biweekly ritual is eval calibration. This is where the team takes a hard look at whether the evaluation framework itself is still valid. Evals can go stale in ways that are really insidious. Maybe you built a great eval for customer service responses six months ago, but since then the product has expanded to handle billing disputes, and your evals don't adequately cover that domain. During eval calibration, the team reviews a sample of production outputs that scored well on evals and a sample that scored poorly, and they ask human experts whether those scores feel right. If there's meaningful disagreement between the automated evals and human judgment, you need to recalibrate. This is painstaking work but it's absolutely foundational. Evals that you can't trust are worse than no evals, because they give you false confidence.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: Core Rituals and Cadence (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: That's a point that doesn't get made often enough. Stale evals create a false sense of security, which might actually be more dangerous than no evals at all because at least with no evals you know you're flying blind. What about the monthly rhythm?
chapter: SEGMENT 2: Core Rituals and Cadence (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: The monthly ritual is a cross-functional operating retrospective. This brings together AI Product Ops, product management, engineering, data science, customer success, and trust and safety. chapter: SEGMENT 2: Core Rituals and Cadence (10 minutes)

chapter: SEGMENT 2: Core Rituals and Cadence (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: Let's shift to the release pipeline, because this is where AI products are fundamentally different from traditional software. In traditional product ops, a release is a code deploy. What does a release look like in an AI product?
chapter: SEGMENT 3: The AI Release Pipeline (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: In an AI product, you have at least five different types of artifacts that you're continuously releasing, and this is what makes it so different. You have prompt changes, which are modifications to the instructions you give the model. You have policy changes, which are updates to the guardrails, filters, and business rules that govern what the AI can and can't do. You have retrieval configuration changes, like modifying the chunking strategy, updating the vector index, changing the re-ranking weights. You have model routing changes, like deciding to send certain query types to a different model or updating the model version. And you have workflow orchestration changes, like adding a new step to an agentic pipeline or modifying the conditions under which the system escalates to a human. Each of these is a release, each can materially change the system's behavior, and each needs to go through a disciplined pipeline. But here's the critical insight: these changes move at very different velocities. Prompt tweaks might happen multiple times a day. Model routing changes might happen monthly. Your release pipeline needs to handle all of these cadences with appropriate rigor for each.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: The AI Release Pipeline (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: So you've got this multi-speed release pipeline. How do you put appropriate gates on each type of change without creating a bottleneck that kills your iteration speed?
chapter: SEGMENT 3: The AI Release Pipeline (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: This is the central design challenge, and the answer is a tiered gate structure. Every change, regardless of type, goes through pre-deploy eval gates. But the depth and breadth of those gates varies by the risk profile of the change. A prompt tweak that modifies the tone of a non-critical informational response might need to pass a focused eval suite of maybe fifty test cases in the relevant domain. A model routing change that affects every user interaction needs to pass the full eval suite, which could be thousands of test cases across every workflow and edge case you've cataloged. The key is to automate this completely. When an engineer or a PM pushes a prompt change, the CI pipeline automatically runs the appropriate eval suite, compares the results against the baseline, and either greenlights the deploy or blocks it with a clear explanation of what failed. No human should be manually running evals and eyeballing results. That doesn't scale and it introduces inconsistency. The eval gates should be as automatic and rigorous as unit tests in traditional software, because they serve the same function: they're your regression safety net.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: The AI Release Pipeline (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: What about blast-radius controls? Even if something passes evals, you might not want to roll it out to everyone at once.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: The AI Release Pipeline (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: Absolutely, and this is where AI releases really need to borrow from the best practices of progressive delivery. Every non-trivial change should go through staged rollout. You start with an internal dogfood cohort, then maybe five percent of traffic, then twenty-five, then fifty, then full rollout. At each stage, you're monitoring the same metrics you track in your daily and weekly rituals: confidence scores, override rates, escalation rates, task-completion rates, latency, cost. And you have automated rollback triggers. If any monitored metric degrades beyond a predefined threshold during a rollout stage, the system automatically reverts to the previous configuration and alerts the team. This is not optional. I've seen teams that do careful evals before deploy but then roll out to everyone at once. That's like having a great fire alarm but no sprinkler system. The blast-radius controls are your sprinklers. They contain the damage while you figure out what happened.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: The AI Release Pipeline (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: Let's talk about the rollback piece specifically. In traditional software, rolling back is conceptually simple: you redeploy the previous version. Is rollback more complicated in an AI context?
chapter: SEGMENT 3: The AI Release Pipeline (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: Significantly more complicated, and teams underestimate this. In traditional software, a rollback is essentially stateless. You deploy the old code, the old code runs, done. In AI products, there can be state implications. If you changed a prompt and the model generated outputs that were stored, those outputs don't disappear when you roll back the prompt. If you updated a retrieval index and the AI used the new index to answer questions and those answers were cached or used as training data, you have downstream contamination. So rollback in AI requires thinking about three layers. The first layer is configuration rollback: reverting the prompt, policy, retrieval config, or model routing to the previous state. This should be instant and automated. The second layer is output remediation: identifying any outputs generated by the changed configuration that may need to be flagged, reviewed, or corrected. This is harder and often requires manual review. The third layer is downstream impact assessment: understanding whether any outputs from the changed configuration were fed into other systems, used for fine-tuning, or surfaced to customers in ways that persist beyond the rollback. Good AI Product Ops teams have a rollback runbook that covers all three layers, and they rehearse it regularly.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: The AI Release Pipeline (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: That three-layer rollback framework is really valuable. The idea that you can't just flip a switch and pretend the change never happened is something a lot of teams learn the hard way. How does version control work for all these different artifact types?
chapter: SEGMENT 3: The AI Release Pipeline (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: Every artifact type needs to be versioned and every version needs to be tied to its eval results. So you end up with what I call a configuration state record: at any point in time, you can reconstruct exactly what combination of prompt version, policy version, retrieval config version, and model version was running, and you can see the eval results that were produced when that combination was tested. This is your audit trail. When something goes wrong, you can diff the current configuration state against the last known good state and identify exactly what changed. When a customer asks why the system behaved differently last week versus this week, you can answer with precision. Some teams store this in a dedicated configuration management system, some use git-based approaches with structured files, some use feature flag platforms that have been extended for AI artifacts. The specific tooling matters less than the discipline of maintaining a complete, queryable history of every configuration change and its associated eval results.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: The AI Release Pipeline (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: Let's talk about when things go wrong, because they will go wrong. AI products have failure modes that traditional software doesn't have. What does a mature incident response process look like for AI products?
chapter: SEGMENT 4: Incident Response and Learning Loops (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: The first thing to internalize is that AI incidents are categorically different from traditional software incidents. A traditional incident is usually binary: the system is up or it's down, the feature works or it doesn't. AI incidents are often subtle and gradual. The system is technically working, but its outputs are slowly degrading, or it's confidently wrong in a specific domain, or it's behaving well on average but terribly for a particular customer segment. This means your detection has to be more sophisticated. You can't just rely on error rates and latency. You need to monitor output quality continuously, and that brings us back to evals running in production, not just in the pre-deploy pipeline. Once you detect an incident, the response framework has four phases: contain, communicate, investigate, and institutionalize. Each phase has specific requirements that are different from traditional incident management.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: Incident Response and Learning Loops (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: Walk us through each phase. Let's start with containment.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: Incident Response and Learning Loops (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: Containment in AI means reducing the blast radius immediately. The options depend on the severity and the nature of the incident. At the highest severity, you might route all affected traffic to a fallback model or a deterministic rule-based system. That's your circuit breaker. One level down, you might tighten confidence thresholds so that more cases get escalated to human review instead of being handled autonomously. One level further, you might disable specific capabilities or workflows while keeping the rest of the system running. The key principle is that containment should be fast and should err on the side of caution. You can always loosen the constraints once you understand the problem. The worst thing you can do is spend two hours debating whether the issue is bad enough to warrant containment while customers are being affected. So you need pre-defined containment playbooks for different scenario types. Your team should be able to execute containment within minutes, not hours, and the triggering criteria should be as unambiguous as possible.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: Incident Response and Learning Loops (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: And then communication. I imagine that's tricky with AI incidents because the nature of the problem can be hard to explain to customers.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: Incident Response and Learning Loops (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: This is one of the hardest parts. With a traditional outage, you can say "the system is down, we're working on it, here's our ETA." With an AI quality incident, you're often saying something much more nuanced, like "the system may have provided inaccurate recommendations in certain scenarios over the past six hours." That's a harder message to craft and a harder message for customers to process. The communication framework I recommend has three elements. First, acknowledge the issue promptly and specifically. Don't be vague. If the problem is that your AI was generating incorrect financial calculations for a specific type of query, say that. Customers lose trust faster when they feel you're being evasive than when they hear about a specific, bounded problem. Second, explain the impact scope. How many customers were affected, what time period, what types of interactions. Customers need to know whether they need to go back and check their own work. Third, describe the remediation plan, not just "we're fixing it" but what specifically you're doing and what customers should do in the meantime. This communication should come from the product team, not from a generic support channel, because it requires product judgment to frame accurately.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: Incident Response and Learning Loops (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: Okay, now investigation. You mentioned that root cause analysis has to span multiple layers. What does that look like?
chapter: SEGMENT 4: Incident Response and Learning Loops (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: AI root cause analysis needs to examine three layers, and the mistake I see most often is teams that stop at the first layer and declare the root cause prematurely. The first layer is the model layer. Did the model itself produce a bad output? Was it a hallucination, a capability limitation, a regression from a model update? You investigate this by running the offending inputs through the model in a controlled environment and examining the outputs. The second layer is the data layer. Was the model given bad context? Did the retrieval pipeline surface irrelevant or outdated documents? Was the user's query misinterpreted before being passed to the model? I'd say a majority of AI quality incidents that get blamed on "the model hallucinated" are actually data layer problems. The model did the best it could with the context it was given, but the context was wrong or incomplete. The third layer is the workflow layer. Was the orchestration logic flawed? Did the system fail to escalate when it should have? Did a policy filter remove information the model needed? Were the prompts inadequately constraining the output format? You have to investigate all three layers for every significant incident. And importantly, you need to distinguish between the proximate cause and the systemic cause. The proximate cause might be "a stale document in the retrieval index." The systemic cause might be "we have no automated freshness check on our document index." Fixing the proximate cause resolves the incident. Fixing the systemic cause prevents the class of incident.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: Incident Response and Learning Loops (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: And then the final phase, institutionalize. What does that mean concretely?
chapter: SEGMENT 4: Incident Response and Learning Loops (10 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: Institutionalization is the learning loop that closes the whole process, and it's where most teams fall short. There are three concrete outputs from every significant incident. First, a new eval test case. Every incident should produce at least one test case that, if it had existed before the incident, would have caught the problem. This test case goes into your eval suite permanently. Over time, your eval suite becomes a living record of everything that's ever gone wrong, which is incredibly valuable. Second, a runbook update. If the incident revealed a scenario that your containment playbooks don't cover, update them. If it revealed that your communication templates were inadequate, update those. Third, a verification test. After you fix the root cause, you don't just run your existing evals. You write a specific test that validates the fix, and you run it not just once but continuously going forward. This is the AI equivalent of writing a regression test for a bug fix. The combination of these three outputs means that every incident makes the system more resilient. You're turning operational pain into structural strength. I've seen teams that do this well, and after twelve months their system is remarkably robust, not because they avoided incidents but because they learned from every single one.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: Incident Response and Learning Loops (10 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: Let's talk about the tooling stack. There's an emerging ecosystem of AI ops tools, but also a lot of teams building custom solutions. How do you think about what to build versus what to buy for AI Product Ops?
chapter: SEGMENT 5: Tooling and Dashboards (8 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: The build-versus-buy calculus for AI Product Ops tooling is genuinely tricky right now because the space is moving so fast. Here's my general framework. Buy the commodity layer: observability, log aggregation, basic model monitoring. There are good off-the-shelf tools for tracking model latency, token usage, basic error rates. You shouldn't be building Datadog for AI from scratch. Build the judgment layer: your eval frameworks, your confidence scoring logic, your domain-specific quality rubrics. These encode your product's unique definition of quality, and no generic tool can do this for you. A customer service AI and a code generation AI have completely different quality criteria. Your evals need to reflect your specific product, your specific customers, your specific risk tolerance. And then there's a middle zone for tooling around release pipeline automation, configuration management, and incident workflows. Here, I'd say buy if you find something that's eighty percent of what you need and extend it. Build from scratch only if your requirements are genuinely unique, which they usually aren't.
chapter: SEGMENT 5: Tooling and Dashboards (8 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: What about the dashboard itself? When the AI Product Ops team walks in every morning, what should they be looking at?
chapter: SEGMENT 5: Tooling and Dashboards (8 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: The dashboard needs to be tight and actionable. I've seen teams build beautiful monitoring dashboards with fifty metrics, and they end up being wallpaper that nobody actually uses for decision-making. Here are the essential metrics grouped by purpose. The first group is quality metrics: eval pass rates broken down by workflow and by severity level, confidence score distributions with trend lines, and override rates, meaning how often humans change the AI's output or decision. Override rates are one of the most underrated signals in AI ops. A rising override rate in a specific workflow is often the earliest indicator of a quality problem. The second group is operational metrics: escalation rates and escalation resolution times, time-to-detection for quality issues, and time-to-remediation once an issue is identified. These tell you how well your operational machinery is working. The third group is business impact metrics: cost per outcome, meaning what you're spending in model inference and human review to produce each unit of value; task completion rates, meaning how often the AI successfully completes what the user asked it to do; and customer satisfaction scores specific to AI-powered interactions. These connect your operational performance to business results, which is what your executives care about.
chapter: SEGMENT 5: Tooling and Dashboards (8 minutes)

speaker: ALEX
text: You mentioned confidence-distribution drift as something to watch in the weekly review. Can you explain what that is and why it matters?
chapter: SEGMENT 5: Tooling and Dashboards (8 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: This is one of the most important signals and one that many teams miss entirely. When your AI processes a request, it typically produces some kind of confidence signal, either an explicit score or something you can derive from the model's behavior. If you plot the distribution of those confidence scores over time, you should see a relatively stable shape. Maybe it's bimodal, with a peak of high-confidence routine requests and a smaller peak of lower-confidence edge cases. That's fine. What you watch for is drift in that distribution. If the high-confidence peak is gradually shifting left, meaning the model is becoming less confident on average, something is changing. Maybe the user queries are drifting into new territory the model wasn't designed for. Maybe the retrieval context quality is degrading. Maybe a recent model update introduced subtle regressions. The distribution shift often shows up before any specific eval failure, because it reflects a broad change in the system's operating conditions. So tracking confidence-distribution drift is like monitoring the vital signs of the system. The specific numbers matter less than the trend, and any sudden or sustained shift warrants investigation.
chapter: SEGMENT 5: Tooling and Dashboards (8 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: This is where you need to be very intentional, because the naive approach, which is to bolt on more people and more rituals for each new AI surface, leads to an operational mess. This works when you have one to three AI-powered workflows. Everyone is in the same triage, the same weekly review, the same dashboards. The advantage is consistency and knowledge sharing. text: It typically breaks around four to six AI workflows, or when the workflows are sufficiently different in domain and risk profile that a single triage session can't cover them all meaningfully. But you maintain a central platform team that provides the shared tooling, the eval infrastructure, the release pipeline automation, and the configuration management system. And you maintain a cross-pod monthly retrospective so that learnings flow across the organization. The central AI Product Ops platform team provides self-service tooling: eval frameworks that product teams can configure for their specific domains, release pipeline templates that teams can customize, incident response playbooks that teams can extend, dashboard templates that teams can populate. text: What are the biggest mistakes you see teams make when scaling AI Product Ops?
chapter: SEGMENT 7: Scaling Product Ops as AI Surface Area Grows (8 minutes)

speaker: KEVIN
text: Three common mistakes. First, scaling people before scaling tooling. If your triage process requires someone to manually query three different systems to understand an exception, adding more people just means more people doing manual work. Before you scale the team, automate the data aggregation, the alert correlation, and the routine classification. Your people should be spending their time on judgment and investigation, not on data gathering. Second, losing the learning loops in the handoff. When you go from centralized to federated, there's a real risk that the pods become silos. An incident that happens in the customer service pod might be directly relevant to the document processing pod, but if they don't share learnings, you lose the organizational memory. You have to design explicit cross-pollination mechanisms: shared incident databases, cross-pod participation in monthly retros, rotating assignments where people spend time in a different pod. Third, and this is the subtlest one, confusing coverage with capability. Teams sometimes look at their growing AI surface area and think "we need AI Product Ops coverage for each workflow," and they focus on getting bodies in seats. But what you actually need is capability depth. One excellent Eval Engineer who builds a reusable eval framework is worth more than three junior analysts who run manual quality checks. As you scale, invest disproportionately in the platform capabilities that provide leverage, because that's how you avoid the linear scaling trap where headcount grows proportionally to AI surface area.
